title: Introducing the Dorada Collection
body:
## A New Chapter in Gold

The **Dorada Collection** represents a deep exploration of gold leaf techniques combined with traditional watercolor methods. Each piece in this collection captures the interplay between precious metallic surfaces and organic, flowing pigments.

### The Inspiration

Working with gold leaf has always fascinated me. The way light catches the surface at different angles transforms each piece throughout the day. *Persimmons del Oro* and *Limones del Cobre* are two key works that embody this vision.

### Techniques Used

- Traditional gold leaf application on watercolor paper
- Layered watercolor washes beneath metallic surfaces
- Pencil detailing for organic forms

I hope you enjoy exploring this collection as much as I enjoyed creating it.
excerpt: Exploring the interplay between gold leaf and watercolor in the new Dorada collection.

title: Working with Gold Leaf: Techniques and Tips
body:
## Gold Leaf for Beginners

Gold leaf is one of the most rewarding materials to work with, but it can be intimidating at first. Here are some techniques I've developed over years of practice.

### Materials You'll Need

1. **Gold leaf sheets** - I recommend starting with imitation gold leaf before moving to genuine
2. **Sizing adhesive** - Water-based sizing is easier to control
3. **Soft brushes** - A gilder's tip and a soft mop brush
4. **Burnishing tool** - An agate burnisher works best

### Step-by-Step Process

First, prepare your surface. The paper or canvas must be completely dry and free of dust. Apply a thin, even coat of sizing and wait until it reaches the right tack.

> The key to successful gold leaf application is patience. Rush the sizing and you'll get wrinkles. Wait too long and it won't adhere.

### Common Mistakes

- Applying leaf to wet sizing
- Using too much adhesive
- Not sealing the finished surface

Practice on scrap paper before committing to a final piece. The results are worth the effort.
excerpt: A guide to gold leaf application techniques for artists, from materials to finished piece.

title: Behind the Scenes: Creating Casa de Fuji
body:
## The Story Behind Casa de Fuji

This piece began as a small sketch in my notebook during a quiet afternoon. The image of a traditional Japanese house with Mount Fuji in the background kept returning to me.

### Initial Sketches

I started with pencil studies, working out the composition. The challenge was balancing the intimate scale of the house against the grandeur of the mountain.

### Color Studies

Before committing to the final piece, I created several small color studies:

- **Study 1**: Warm palette with sunset tones
- **Study 2**: Cool blues and grays for a misty morning feel
- **Study 3**: The final direction - a balanced palette that evokes serenity

### The Final Piece

The finished work took several sessions to complete. Each layer of watercolor needed to dry completely before the next could be applied. The architectural details of the house required careful brushwork with a fine-tipped brush.

This piece is part of the Oriental collection and represents my ongoing fascination with Japanese aesthetics.
excerpt: A look at the creative process behind Casa de Fuji, from initial sketches to finished watercolor.

title: Learning Watercolor: My Journey So Far
body:
## Reflections on the Watercolor Medium

Watercolor has been my primary medium for the past few years, and I wanted to share some reflections on what I've learned along the way.

### Why Watercolor?

The transparency and unpredictability of watercolor drew me in. Unlike acrylics or oils, you can't easily cover mistakes. Every brushstroke matters, and the medium teaches you to be decisive.

### Key Lessons

1. **Work light to dark** - Always start with your lightest values
2. **Preserve your whites** - The white of the paper is your brightest highlight
3. **Embrace happy accidents** - Some of the best effects come from letting the water do its thing
4. **Quality materials matter** - Good paper makes more difference than good paint

### Recommended Resources

For anyone starting their watercolor journey, I recommend practicing basic washes before attempting complex subjects. Spend time understanding how water behaves on different papers.

The Botánica collection represents some of my most confident watercolor work to date.
excerpt: Sharing lessons learned from years of watercolor painting, with tips for beginners.

title: The Language of Gold: Understanding the Dorada Palette
body:
## Color Theory Meets Precious Metal

The Dorada collection is built around a specific palette that pairs gold leaf with warm, earthy tones. In this post I want to break down how these color relationships work and why certain combinations feel harmonious.

### Gold as a Color

Gold leaf is not simply "yellow." Depending on the alloy, genuine gold leaf ranges from a cool, almost greenish tone to a deep, warm reddish hue. The standard 23-karat leaf I use sits in a warm, buttery middle ground that pairs beautifully with:

- **Burnt sienna** and **raw umber** for grounding warmth
- **Cadmium lemon** for bright citrus contrast
- **Prussian blue** as a complementary accent

### Building the Dorada Palette

In *Persimmons del Oro*, the warm orange of the fruit naturally echoes the gold, creating a monochromatic warmth. The pencil linework provides a cooler, neutral structure that keeps the composition from feeling overwhelmingly hot.

*Limones del Cobre* takes the opposite approach. The cool yellow-green of the lemons contrasts against the warm copper-gold background, creating tension and visual interest. The title itself nods to this interplay: limones (lemons) against cobre (copper).

### Practical Tips for Your Own Palette

1. **Test on scraps first** - Gold leaf looks different over every base color
2. **Limit your palette** - Three or four colors beside the gold is plenty
3. **Consider the paper tone** - Cream-toned paper warms everything; bright white keeps it crisp
4. **Seal before layering** - If painting over gold, seal it first or the paint will bead

### The Role of Negative Space

One of the most important lessons from the Dorada series is knowing when to stop. Gold is visually loud. Leaving areas of bare paper or simple wash gives the eye a place to rest and makes the gold feel intentional rather than excessive.

I encourage anyone experimenting with metallic materials to study how gold has been used historically, from Byzantine icons to Japanese folding screens. The traditions are rich and the techniques are transferable to contemporary work.
excerpt: A deep dive into the color relationships and palette choices behind the Dorada collection.
